chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
title: Decca sessions of 1942 and the hit "Paella"
summary: Perez of Decca liked "Sopa de Pichon" and "Paella"; well-rehearsed, they cut their records at the Decca studios without overtime.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Okay. Robbins was your publisher for which record label?

I started - I made myself a composer before we - Cugat - that I recorded "El Negro a Reza" and I forgot the title of the other number and then I became a composer for Decca because Mr. Perez asked me. Ahh - he liked "Sopa de Pichon" and "La Paella", so we recorded and became two hits. As a matter of fact, they was playing "La Paella" and "Sopa de Pichon" in Havana and all through Cuba; and we recorded in 1942 and the recording was playing until 1946, that I was there.
In 1942 you did all those recordings?
Like "Tingo-Talango", "Chacumbele" and "El Negro se fue de Rumba" —"El Muerto se fue de Rumba".
"El Muerto se fue de Rumba", "Tingo-Talango", all those numbers.
Now, were they all done in one session, two sessions or three sessions?

Really, the band was so well-rehearsed and they were so acquainted with the arranger, I mean the arrangement; the arrangement was made for us, but we played one or few times. We rehearsed in the daytime and then we go to the studio and cut the numbers there. As a matter of fact, we never pay overtime, we never went overtime to make those recordings.
Do you remember what studio you recorded these at?
That was located in 57th between 6th and 5th.
You don't remember the name of the studio?
